web.title: NCP unveils Tk8.52 lakh crore shadow budget for 2026–27
web.description:
**The National Citizen Party (NCP) has unveiled a shadow budget of Tk 8,52,157 crore for the 2026–27 fiscal year, titled "Bangladesh 2.0: Sustainable Growth through Reform, Employment and Investment", placing strong emphasis on job creation, education, inflation control and investment-led growth.**

The NCP has set key macroeconomic targets, including reducing inflation from 9.2 percent to 8 percent in the next fiscal year and further to 6 percent in the following year. It also aims to raise foreign exchange reserves above $32 billion.

Education and employment remain central, with Tk 1,24,425 crore allocated to the education and technology sector, representing 14.6 percent of the total budget.
Key proposals include school feeding programmes in all government primary schools, a Tk 5,000 crore teacher development fund, nationalisation of 5,000 private schools and expansion of technical institutes in every upazila.

web.title: Growth trap, 16-year high inflation signal deepening crisis for Bangladesh, economists warn
web.description:
According to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook on Tuesday, Bangladesh is projected to become South Asia's slowest-growing economy through 2031. The IMF expects growth to decelerate to 3.2% in the current fiscal year (FY27) and bottom out at 2.2% in FY28, before making a sluggish recovery to roughly 3% by FY31. This trajectory contrasts sharply with the interim government's five-year strategic framework published in August, which sets an ambitious growth target of 8.5% by FY31.
Compounding the growth slowdown, the IMF projected average inflation to reach 10.9% this fiscal year, a 16-year high and nearly double the 6% rate forecast six months ago. Bangladesh has already endured inflation exceeding 8% for four consecutive years.
Zahid Hussain, former lead economist at the World Bank's Dhaka office, said the IMF has provided a baseline projection that could materialise if the government fails to deliver on its promised reforms or restorations in three areas – banking, energy, and business regulation.
Fahmida Khatun, a distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue, said the downgrade reflected a prolonged slowdown and high inflation since mid-2022. She said policy mistakes, including a 6-9% interest rate cap, and reform inertia had made matters worse, and that the Middle East war had made the situation more critical.

She said the main reasons behind the weak forecast are a prolonged slowdown in economic activity, low growth and high inflation since mid-2022. A lack of appropriate policies, at times wrong ones such as the 6-9% interest rate cap, and reluctance to carry out reforms have made matters worse, Fahmida said.

Fahmida said the government should keep monetary policy tight to contain inflation, which hits the poor and low-income people hardest. It should also follow austerity measures, she said, because its revenue is not rising amid low investment and high inflation.
"Now, the government should not focus on growth; its core focus should be on controlling inflation, which will help the poor and contribute to a cut in the cost of doing business," she said.

web.title: BRAC University dialogue explores Bangladesh’s FY2026-27 budget priorities
web.description:
**BRAC University hosted a dialogue on Bangladesh's national budget for FY2026-27 at its Merul Badda campus on Thursday, bringing together economists, academics, students and professionals to discuss the country's economic priorities and challenges surrounding budget implementation.**
Organised by BRAC Business School (BBS), the dialogue covered banking sector stability, revenue mobilisation, inflation, taxation, energy security, public expenditure, investment and employment generation, according to a press release.
Professor Salehuddin Ahmed of BBS, former governor of Bangladesh Bank and former adviser to the Government of Bangladesh, identified restoring confidence in the banking sector as an important priority. He highlighted the need for institutional reforms in the financial sector, alongside improvements in revenue collection, tax administration, accountability and expenditure management. He also emphasised the importance of maintaining adequate focus on health, education and social protection.

Delivering the keynote address, Professor M Fouzul Kabir Khan of BBS, Director of BRAC University's Centre for Energy and Logistics (CEL) and a former adviser to the Government of Bangladesh, discussed inflation, taxation, energy security and fiscal management.

web.title: As salaries run out in 20 days, people turn to borrowing
web.description:
The country's inflation figures show how prices continue to rise. Data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) show that overall inflation stood at 8.34% in September 2026, up from 8.26% in August. Food inflation rose from 7.02% to 7.22%, while non-food inflation edged down from 9.32% to 9.3%.
Average inflation over the 12 months to September 2026 was 8.65%, compared with 9.45% in the preceding 12 months. A falling inflation rate does not necessarily mean falling prices, it means prices are rising more slowly. Households therefore continue paying more for goods and services than they did before.
Mahtab Uddin, assistant professor of Economics at the University of Dhaka and Honorary Research Director at the South Asian Network on Economic Modelling (SANEM), believes Bangladesh's inflation problem must be understood in the context of its monetary and fiscal policy decisions.
"While countries such as Britain and India raised interest rates to contain inflation, Bangladesh failed to tighten monetary policy sufficiently or at the right time," he said. "Continued liquidity support for distressed banks and expansionary fiscal policy added to inflationary pressures."

The consequences are particularly severe for lower-income households, which spend a larger share of their earnings on necessities.
"When prices rise and real wages fail to keep pace, people are forced to make difficult choices," Mahtab said, "Families may stop buying fish, meat or fruit, switch to less nutritious food or reduce spending on their children's education."
Such adjustments can have consequences beyond the monthly budget, affecting nutrition, education and long-term economic mobility.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its October 2026 issue of Regional Economic Outlook for Asia and the Pacific, reported that nearly 29% of highly educated young people in Bangladesh are unemployed. The report also warned that AI could exert downward pressure equivalent to 2% of aggregate labour demand in Bangladesh.

web.title: IMF warns Bangladesh's inflation may hit 10.9% in FY27, highest in 16 years
web.description:
**Bangladesh is heading for a possible 16-year high in inflation, with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) today (13 October) projecting it to reach 10.9% in the current FY27 fiscal year, a sharp reversal from the 6% forecast it made just six months ago.**
Bangladesh last recorded a similar annual average in FY2010-11, when inflation reached 10.92%, according to Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) data.

The easing continued into the new fiscal year, with monthly inflation slipping from 8.32% in July to 8.26% in August before rising again to 8.34% in September, BBS data show.

The World Bank, meanwhile, projected in its October 2026 Bangladesh Development Update that inflation will remain elevated at 8.6% in FY27.
It cited recent increases in domestic energy prices, persistent supply-side constraints, expansionary fiscal policy and a shift towards a less contractionary monetary policy stance.
